Received 23 February 1987. accepted 15 January 1988 INTRODUCTION On the eastern side of the South Island of New Zealand and the adjacent Chatham Rise and Campbell Plateau, there are several major centres of late Tertiary alkalic igneous volcanism, which show a general decrease in age towards the southeast (Adams 1981). As there appears to be no relationship between this activity and the plate boundaries, a linear mantle source has been proposed (Adams 1981; Wellman 1983). Four of these centres in South Island were selected for paleomagnetic study: the Dunedin volcano, the Lyttelton volcano, the Akaroa volcano, and the Diamond Harbour Group (Fig. I). These all lie in regions which are considered not to have been affected by later tectonic activity (Walcott 1984). Three have already been the subject of paleomagnetic study: Dunedin (Coombs & Hatherton 1959), Akaroa (Evans 1970), and StoddartFormation of the Diamond Harbour Group (Evans 19

on (this study) marking the top of subchron 4Ar-2. From the mean K-Ar dates calculated for the section (Evans 1970) the mean age for the bottom of the section (this study) is 9.0 ±0.2 Ma and for the top is 8.6 ± 0.2 Ma. This makes correlation of the top normal period with subchron 4Ar-2 (8.80 - 8.87 Ma) the most likely (Fig. 10). This was the correla­ tion favoured by Evans (1970). The lower N-R tran­ sition will correlate with the top of chron 5 and the reversed interval found by Evans (1970) at about 70 m above sea level will correspond to subchron 5-1. DIAMOND HARBOUR GROUP The last stages of volcanism on Banks Peninsula were fairly localised eruptions (SewellI988), often infilling valleys eroded in the earlier Lyttelton flows. The activity was mainly centred around Quail Island and the Diamond Harbour area. Liggett & Gregg (1965) divided these late alkali basalts into three formations which together comprised their Diamond Harbour Group. The Church Formation usually has well-developed columnar jointing in its flows, whereas the Kaioruru Formation appears coarse grained, often forming pahoehoe flows, and the Stoddart Formation forms aa flows with well-developed flow breccias. The three formations are on the shore at Church Bay, with angular unconformities

le position. Although all of the large volcanoes have probably undergone some subsidence since activity ceased (Well man 1983; Weaver & Sewell 1986), there is no evidence of any major tectonic disturbance 10 the lava flows, and quaquaversal dips are preserved in all except for the western edge of the Dunedin volcano (Coombs 1983). Thus a tectonic origin for the far and near sidedness of the two younger centres may be discounted. Although the fact that the reversed VGPsseem to be further from the geocentric axial dipole position might suggest that some of the rocks possess a hard secondary component that has not been isolated by AF demagnetisation up 10 only 50 mT, sister samples which were demagnetised up to 200 mT for paleointensity studies (Sherwood & Shaw 1986) showed no such evidence of a hard secondary component. It appears therefore that the reason for the significant differences between the Diamond Harbour and Akaroa VGPs and the geocentric axial dipole VGP is that the interval sampled in each case was not long enough to cancel out the effects of secular variation. This is not surprising in the Diamond Harbour Group pole, as this is dominated by the semi-intermediate directions from the Stoddart Formation, which must have erupted in a short period of time. Samples were taken from S7 flows on the Lighthouse Road section between 340 and 670 m above sea level (Table 3, Fig. 7). Only flows which were fresh and clearly in situ were sampled. Exposure was better in the top part of the section - only nine flows were sampled in the bottom 160 m. All flows dip at about 100 to the south, away from the centre of the volcano. The flows sampled were all basalt and hawaiite aa flows, with rubbly tops and bottoms and massive centres. Only one flow (ZBA51) did not have a stable NRM. The top flow (ZBA 1) had some cores with a very large secondary component superimposed upon the NRM. This is interpreted as being caused by a lightning strike. It was quite easily removed by AF demagnetisation to leave a reversed NRM. Samples from flow ZBA38 also have a strong secondary component; when this is removed the NRM component remaining has a slightly anomalous direction. directional_or_weak_substitution_warning.excerpt: s· A bstract Orientated samples were collected from 135 sites in 4 centres of Miocene alkali volcanic activity on the South Island of New Zealand: the Dunedin volcano, the Lyttelton volcano, theAkaroa volcano, and the Diamond Harbour Group. The natural remanent magnetisation (NRM) was measured using stepwise alternating field demagnetisation. From the results of at least three specimens a mean site NRM direction was calculated where possible. For each of the four centres a magnetostratigraphy has been determined. By comparing this with previously published K-Ar ages it has been possible to suggest correlations with the magnetic polarity timescale. The mean virtual geomagnetic poles (VGP) for the four centres, oldest to youngest, are: Dunedin volcano 86°.6N, 357°.0E; Lyttelton volcano 87°.7N, 086°.3E; Akaroa volcano 79°.7N, 137°.6E; and Diamond HarbourGroup68°.6N,012°.IE.Evenafterrotation of the VGPs back to their original positions, using hotspot-relative rotations, the two youngest VGPs deviate significantly from the geocentric axial dipole position. The irregular nature of volcanic activity has apparently caused a bias towards a particular direction. PALAEOMAGNETTC DATA Hand samples and drilled cores were oriented in the field at a variety of sites (Fig. i) from Dunnet Head to south of the Moray Firth. The samples were cut into 2-5 cm diameter, 2*5 cm high cylindrical specimens and their initial magnetisation was measured using astatic and spinner magnetometers. One representative pilot specimen was chosen from each site and subjected to routine incremental thermal demagnetisation (Tarling, 1971) up to 650°C in order to determine their blocking temperature spectra. Thermally induced chemical changes of the magnetic minerals during heating were monitored by measuring the susceptibility (Collinson et al. 1963) after each temperature increment. On the basis of the behaviour of the pilot specimens, the remaining specimens were all heated to 300°C and their magnetisation remeasured. As titanomagnetites have Curie points lower than 6oo°C, most of the collection was then heated to between 600 and 650°C, and remeasured, in order to examine the high temperature remanence carried by haematite alone. STORETVEDT Institute of Geophysics, University of Bergen, 5000 Bergen, Norway SYNOPSIS Palaeomagnetic results from the Sarclet Sandstone Formation, stratig- raphically positioned near the base of the Old Red Sandstone (ORS) sequence of Caithness, suggest the presence of two different axes of magnetization, with Dec. 211, Inc. 33 and Dec. 191, Inc. 6 respectively. The most steeply inclined magnetization is in correspondence with results from Scottish Lower Old Red Sandstone volcanics indicating that the age of the Sarclet Sandstone dates from the topmost Silurian-lowermost Devonian. The abundant clasts of basalts in the underlying Sarclet Conglomerate give further substance to the notion that the Lower Old Red Sandstone volcanics, which have a wide distribution in central and southern regions of Scotland, also occurred in the Caithness/Moray Firth area. It is concluded therefore that the Orcadian Basin developed concur­ rently with the ORS basins of the Midland Valley and the Scottish Borders. The abundant clasts of basalts in the underlying Sarclet Conglomerate give further substance to the notion that the Lower Old Red Sandstone volcanics, which have a wide distribution in central and southern regions of Scotland, also occurred in the Caithness/Moray Firth area. It is concluded therefore that the Orcadian Basin developed concur­ rently with the ORS basins of the Midland Valley and the Scottish Borders. It is inferred that the second magnetization (with shallow inclination) was imposed at around Middle Devonian, but owing to a relatively early silica cementation the Sarclet Sandstone was not suscepti­ ble to acquiring the "Permian" magnetization overprint that is strongly developed in the higher stratigraphic units of the Caithness Old Red Sandstone. This succession, which has a thickness of around 4 km, is preceded by the Sarclet Group consisting of nearly 450 m of conglomerate and sandstone/mudstone (Donovan et al. 1974). Due to the mostly barren nature of this basal group its age has been uncertain but, based on some moderately or poorly preserved spore assemblages, a topmost Lower Devonian (Emsian) origin has recently been suggested (Collins and Donovan 1977). SAMPLING AND TREATMENT Sampling was restricted to Eastern Mainland Orkney and the adjacent islands of Burray, S. Ronaldsay, Black Holm (Copinsay) and Shapinsay (Fig. 1). A total of 173 specimens from 21 sites have been progressively demagnetised, the majority, 148, by thermal demagnetisation while a further 25 were demagnetised by alternat­ ing field (A.F.). Of these 21 sites, 10 are from the lavas within the Eday Flags, including one site in the baked contact in the Eday Flags immediately below (Site 19). Eday Group sediments are represented by the Lower Eday Sandstone (Sites 11 to 13), Middle Eday Sandstone (Sites 16 to 18 and 24), Eday Marls (Sites 22, 30 and 31) and Upper Eday Sandstone (Site 21). Of the four sites in the Middle Eday Sandstone, two (16 and 18) give statistically uninterpretable component distribu­ tions although several samples have two peaks in the T B spectrum, cutting off at approximately 580°C and 680°C. These two remanence components, carried in magnetite and hematite respectively, are in different directions. The remaining two sites have a stable, high-T B remanence with a maximum TB of 675°-685°C, suggesting it to be held in hematite. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: from the Eday Group (upper Middle Old Red Sandstone), Orkney; including 85 from a contemporaneous lava and its baked contact, and 88 from Eday Group sediments. There is general agreement between stable NRM directions in the lava and its baked contact in the Eday Flags, which together give a mean direction after tectonic dip correction of D = 191°, I = 41°, corresponding to a palaeomagnetic pole at 8°N, 167°E. This may provide an approximate estimate of the upper Middle Devonian palaeomagnetic pole relative to Orkney. All the palaeomagnetically stable sites elsewhere in the Eday Group sediments show a high blocking-temperature (T B) component which give an in situ mean direction of D = 191°, I = —20°, corresponding to a palaeomagnetic pole position of 41°N, 163°E. This component is believed to be of secondary origin, and probably relates to a late Palaeozoic remagnetisation, as is apparently the case elsewhere in the Devonian of Europe and the USSR. However, there is insufficient between-site varia­ tion in tectonic dip to ascertain incontrovertibly the relative ages of remanence acquisition and deformation, which is generally considered to predate deposition of the Upper ORS. A single site in the Eday Marls shows two poorly-defined ancient components, a low-T B one in approximate agreement with the result from the lavas and a high-TB component in a similar orientation to that found elsewhere in the Eday Group sediments. PSIS This study presents the progressive demagnetisation results for 173 specimens from the Eday Group (upper Middle Old Red Sandstone), Orkney; including 85 from a contemporaneous lava and its baked contact, and 88 from Eday Group sediments. There is general agreement between stable NRM directions in the lava and its baked contact in the Eday Flags, which together give a mean direction after tectonic dip correction of D = 191°, I = 41°, corresponding to a palaeomagnetic pole at 8°N, 167°E. This may provide an approximate estimate of the upper Middle Devonian palaeomagnetic pole relative to Orkney. All the palaeomagnetically stable sites elsewhere in the Eday Group sediments show a high blocking-temperature (T B) component which give an in situ mean direction of D = 191°, I = —20°, corresponding to a palaeomagnetic pole position of 41°N, 163°E. This component is believed to be of secondary origin, and probably relates to a late Palaeozoic remagnetisation, as is apparently the case elsewhere in the Devonian of Europe and the USSR. However, there is insufficient between-site varia­ tion in tectonic dip to ascertain incontrovertibly the relative ages of remanence acquisition and deformation, which is generally considered to predate deposition of the Upper ORS. GENERAL GEOLOGY AND SAMPLING At the base of the Hoy Sandstone of Upper Old Red Sandstone age (Sedgwick and Murchison 1828; Wilson et al. 1935; Halliday et al. 1977) a volcanic horizon is exposed at a few localities notably in the northern part of the island (Fig. 1). The volcanicity was of explosive character and an ashy deposit with thicknesses ranging upward to c. 15 m was laid down prior to lava outpouring. In the various lava outcrops only one flow is recognized at any one locality, and the petrography is always that of an olivine basalt with phenocrysts of olivine, pyroxene and feldspar (Wilson et al. 1935). Faults occur between the separate igneous exposures, and from field evidence it is impossible to be certain of the precise stratigraphical relation between the outcrops. In northern Hoy the volcanics rest on Middle Old Red Sandstone strata and between these sediments and the overlying Hoy Sandstone there is a fairly marked tectonic unconformity. Apart from the Old Man of Hoy exposure, which shows evidence of some erosion of the lava prior to deposition of the Hoy Sandstone, the slaggy and reddish upper part of the flow(s) is

rests directly upon the Lower Eday Sandstone forming a pronounced baked contact zone. The sampling sites are distributed throughout the whole thickness of the lava as well as being located at various distances, up to 1 m, away from the lava/sediment contact. At Rackwick sampling was less systematic due to break-down of the drilling equipment, and it was also hampered by the difficulty of obtaining good sites for hand sampling. A total of 76 specimens have been analysed and 41 of these have yielded remanence directions forming distinct groupings. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: versity of Bergen, Allegt. 70, 5000 Bergen, Norway 2Dept. of Earth Sciences, Memorial University of Newfoundland, Canada SYNOPSIS The palaeomagnetic record of Devonian Volcanics of Hoy (—370 Ma), occurring at the base of the Hoy Sandstone (Upper Devonian), exhibits coherent groups of remanence directions. An original shallow magnetiza­ tion axis, repeatedly reported from studies of Old Red Sandstone rocks of Caithness, is confirmed, but the data suggest also that the tectonic unconformity between the Middle Devonian strata (upon which the volcanics rest) and the Hoy Sandstone originated at around the time of the volcanic activity. A secondary magnetization of inferred Permian age has been uncovered from the underlying Middle Devonian sediments (Lower Eday Sandstone). This overprinted component of magnetization, which is a pronounced feature in various Caithness rocks, is reported here for the first time for Orkney rocks. The Permian overprinting event is held responsible for the demonstrable loss of argon in the Devonian volcanics, rendering also the K/Ar ages for other igneous rocks in the region highly suspect. An original shallow magnetiza­ tion axis, repeatedly reported from studies of Old Red Sandstone rocks of Caithness, is confirmed, but the data suggest also that the tectonic unconformity between the Middle Devonian strata (upon which the volcanics rest) and the Hoy Sandstone originated at around the time of the volcanic activity. A secondary magnetization of inferred Permian age has been uncovered from the underlying Middle Devonian sediments (Lower Eday Sandstone). This overprinted component of magnetization, which is a pronounced feature in various Caithness rocks, is reported here for the first time for Orkney rocks. The Permian overprinting event is held responsible for the demonstrable loss of argon in the Devonian volcanics, rendering also the K/Ar ages for other igneous rocks in the region highly suspect. Complex multiphase magnetiza­ tions have been uncovered in most of these cases, and for various Caithness rocks a substantial fraction of the original Devonian remanence appears to have been erased during Permo-Mesozoic remagnetization. On the whole, the total palaeomagnetic record has gradually become better understood and as a conse­ quence a number of potential applications of the results to local geological problems can now be envisaged. In the present contribution we give an account of the magnetization history of Devonian volcanics and baked Devonian sediments from Hoy, Orkney. inal titano-magnetite (TM) grains of the Devonian tuff layer of Hoy have undergone a complete oxidation in that all TM particles now tend to consist of haematite and rutile. The more severe oxidation state of the tuff, as compared to that of the lavas, is in part attributed to its fairly porous character. Thus, given rocks like the Orkney volcanics, one must anticipate a lengthy magnetization record of unknown duration. The palaeomagnetic structure of such rocks would normally be a complex one (as was also demonstrated in the earlier study), but provided individual palaeomagnetic components can be successfully extracted, important information on the geological history of the region might be deduced. In view of the progress in palaeomagnetic instrumentation and techniques over the past 15 years, it was decided to re-assess the palaeomagnetism of the Hoy volcanics with the hope of achieving more information than that obtained in the original study. The present investigation is believed to have been quite successful in this respect, and the results appear to have interesting implications for tectonic and age problems. M. STORETVEDT 1 '2 AND A. H. MELAND 1 1 Institute of Geophysics, University of Bergen, Allegt. 70, 5000 Bergen, Norway 2Dept. of Earth Sciences, Memorial University of Newfoundland, Canada SYNOPSIS The palaeomagnetic record of Devonian Volcanics of Hoy (—370 Ma), occurring at the base of the Hoy Sandstone (Upper Devonian), exhibits coherent groups of remanence directions. An original shallow magnetiza­ tion axis, repeatedly reported from studies of Old Red Sandstone rocks of Caithness, is confirmed, but the data suggest also that the tectonic unconformity between the Middle Devonian strata (upon which the volcanics rest) and the Hoy Sandstone originated at around the time of the volcanic activity. A secondary magnetization of inferred Permian age has been uncovered from the underlying Middle Devonian sediments (Lower Eday Sandstone). This overprinted component of magnetization, which is a pronounced feature in various Caithness rocks, is reported here for the first time for Orkney rocks. The Permian overprinting event is held responsible for the demonstrable loss of argon in the Devonian volcanics, rendering also the K/Ar ages for other igneous rocks in the region highly suspect. INTRODUCTION In recent years quite a few palaeomagnetic studies have been undertaken on rocks from the Orcadian Basin (for example, Storetvedt and Petersen 1972; Tarling et al. 1976; Turner 1977; Turner et al. 1978; Storetvedt et al. 1978; Storetvedt and Carmichael 1979; Storetvedt and Torsvik 1983). Complex multiphase magnetiza­ tions have been uncovered in most of these cases, and for various Caithness rocks a substantial fraction of the original Devonian remanence appears to have been erased during Permo-Mesozoic remagnetization. On the whole, the total palaeomagnetic record has gradually become better understood and as a conse­ quence a number of potential applications of the results to local geological problems can now be envisaged. In the present contribution we give an account of the magnetization history of Devonian volcanics and baked Devonian sediments from Hoy, Orkney. In a previous study of the Orkney volcanics (Storetvedt and Petersen 1972) it was found that these rocks (including partly the exposures dealt with in the present study) provide a striking example of extensive low temper

inal titano-magnetite (TM) grains of the Devonian tuff layer of Hoy have undergone a complete oxidation in that all TM particles now tend to consist of haematite and rutile. The more severe oxidation state of the tuff, as compared to that of the lavas, is in part attributed to its fairly porous character. Thus, given rocks like the Orkney volcanics, one must anticipate a lengthy magnetization record of unknown duration. The palaeomagnetic structure of such rocks would normally be a complex one (as was also demonstrated in the earlier study), but provided individual palaeomagnetic components can be successfully extracted, important information on the geological history of the region might be deduced. In view of the progress in palaeomagnetic instrumentation and techniques over the past 15 years, it was decided to re-assess the palaeomagnetism of the Hoy volcanics with the hope of achieving more information than that obtained in the original study. The present investigation is believed to have been quite successful in this respect, and the results appear to have interesting implications for tectonic and age problems. GENERAL GEOLOGY AND SAMPLING At the base of the Hoy Sandstone of Upper Old Red Sandstone age (Sedgwick and Murchison 1828; Wilson et al. 1935; Halliday et al. 1977) a volcanic horizon is exposed at a few localities notably in the northern part of the island (Fig. 1). The volcanicity was of explosive character and an ashy deposit with thicknesses ranging upward to c. 15 m was laid down prior to lava outpouring. In the various lava outcrops only one flow is recognized at any one locality, and the petrography is always that of an olivine basalt with phenocrysts of olivine, pyroxene and feldspar (Wilson et al. 1935). An original shallow magnetiza­ tion axis, repeatedly reported from studies of Old Red Sandstone rocks of Caithness, is confirmed, but the data suggest also that the tectonic unconformity between the Middle Devonian strata (upon which the volcanics rest) and the Hoy Sandstone originated at around the time of the volcanic activity. A secondary magnetization of inferred Permian age has been uncovered from the underlying Middle Devonian sediments (Lower Eday Sandstone). This overprinted component of magnetization, which is a pronounced feature in various Caithness rocks, is reported here for the first time for Orkney rocks. The Permian overprinting event is held responsible for the demonstrable loss of argon in the Devonian volcanics, rendering also the K/Ar ages for other igneous rocks in the region highly suspect. rinting event is held responsible for the demonstrable loss of argon in the Devonian volcanics, rendering also the K/Ar ages for other igneous rocks in the region highly suspect. INTRODUCTION In recent years quite a few palaeomagnetic studies have been undertaken on rocks from the Orcadian Basin (for example, Storetvedt and Petersen 1972; Tarling et al. 1976; Turner 1977; Turner et al. 1978; Storetvedt et al. 1978; Storetvedt and Carmichael 1979; Storetvedt and Torsvik 1983). Complex multiphase magnetiza­ tions have been uncovered in most of these cases, and for various Caithness rocks a substantial fraction of the original Devonian remanence appears to have been erased during Permo-Mesozoic remagnetization. On the whole, the total palaeomagnetic record has gradually become better understood and as a conse­ quence a number of potential applications of the results to local geological problems can now be envisaged. In the present contribution we give an account of the magnetization history of Devonian volcanics and baked Devonian sediments from Hoy, Orkney. In a previous study of the Orkney volcanics (Storetvedt and Petersen 1972) it was found that these rocks (including partly the exposures dealt with in the present study) provide a striking example of extensive low temper

inal titano-magnetite (TM) grains of the Devonian tuff layer of Hoy have undergone a complete oxidation in that all TM particles now tend to consist of haematite and rutile. The more severe oxidation state of the tuff, as compared to that of the lavas, is in part attributed to its fairly porous character. Thus, given rocks like the Orkney volcanics, one must anticipate a lengthy magnetization record of unknown duration. The palaeomagnetic structure of such rocks would normally be a complex one (as was also demonstrated in the earlier study), but provided individual palaeomagnetic components can be successfully extracted, important information on the geological history of the region might be deduced. In view of the progress in palaeomagnetic instrumentation and techniques over the past 15 years, it was decided to re-assess the palaeomagnetism of the Hoy volcanics with the hope of achieving more information than that obtained in the original study. The present investigation is believed to have been quite successful in this respect, and the results appear to have interesting implications for tectonic and age problems. Introduction Rotation of the Fiji Platform in an anticlockwise direction has been a speculative proposal invoked by the 'spiral nebula' shape of the island group. There has been much discussion of this idea (P.J. Coleman, A. Malahoff, pers. comm.) but very little has appeared in print. They concluded that shear-driven rotation ceased "some considerable time ago" (presumably pre-Pliocene) with present day motion being dominantly transform. PALAEOMAGNETIC RESULTS 35 Gilbraltar, Prospect and Gingenbullen have been radiogenically dated (Evernden and Richards, 1962) and appear to have been intruded during the Jurassic. Recent work by Schmidt (1976) demon- strates that the pole positions from this earlier palaeomagnetic work result from directions in which secondary components have not been entirely elimi- nated, and his mean Jurassic pole position (MJP), from rocks subjected to more severe laboratory treatment, is also shown in Fig. 4. The results of this preliminary study show that there are significant differences in remanent magnetisation directions between different in- trusions into the Sydney Basin. They are consist- ent with a hypothesis that the intrusions into the Sydney Basin came in several pulses (Manwaring, 1963) that can be differentiated, in some cases, by differences in their magnetisation directions and the pole positions calculated from them. Pole positions for other intrusions into the Sydney Basin, of which the directions had been previously determined, (Boesen et al., 1961; Manwaring, 1963) are also shown in Fig. 4. PALAEOMAGNETIC RESULTS 35 Gilbraltar, Prospect and Gingenbullen have been radiogenically dated (Evernden and Richards, 1962) and appear to have been intruded during the Jurassic. Recent work by Schmidt (1976) demon- strates that the pole positions from this earlier palaeomagnetic work result from directions in which secondary components have not been entirely elimi- nated, and his mean Jurassic pole position (MJP), from rocks subjected to more severe laboratory treatment, is also shown in Fig. 4. The results of this preliminary study show that there are significant differences in remanent magnetisation directions between different in- trusions into the Sydney Basin. They are consist- ent with a hypothesis that the intrusions into the Sydney Basin came in several pulses (Manwaring, 1963) that can be differentiated, in some cases, by differences in their magnetisation directions and the pole positions calculated from them. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: Park indicate that these breccias con- solidated in temperatures in excess of 400°C, if we assume that the remanent magnetisation is of thermo- remanent origin and acquired when the magnetic crystals cooled through these blocking temperatures. On the other hand, Hamilton et al (1970) suggest that, on the evidence of coal reflectance figures from fragments found in these breccias, the temper- ature of formation must have been less than 100°C. Two possible solutions to this inconsistency may be considered. Firstly, the temperature within the breccias may have varied from less than 100° to more than 400°C at the time of consolidation. Secondly, chemical alterations in the low temperature ranges may have caused the formation of magnetic minerals, most probably iron oxides that acquired a chemical remanence which itself had higher blocking temperatures. DISCUSSION The mean directions for the nine deposits are shown in Fig. 3. All are normally magnetised except Mogo Hill, Barrenjoey and Peat's Ridge, which are reversely magnetised. It is not possible to tell how much of secular variation has been averaged by the time spread of the samples, as the rate at which the acquisition of the magnetisation spread through the deposits is not known. Hence an unknown, but probably small, secular variation error is likely to be present in all the results. Bearing this in mind, Figure 3. It is not possible to tell how much of secular variation has been averaged by the time spread of the samples, as the rate at which the acquisition of the magnetisation spread through the deposits is not known. Pole positions for other intrusions into the Sydney Basin, of which the directions had been previously determined, (Boesen et al., 1961; Manwaring, 1963) are also shown in Fig. 4. PALAEOMAGNETIC RESULTS 35 Gilbraltar, Prospect and Gingenbullen have been radiogenically dated (Evernden and Richards, 1962) and appear to have been intruded during the Jurassic. Recent work by Schmidt (1976) demon- strates that the pole positions from this earlier palaeomagnetic work result from directions in which secondary components have not been entirely elimi- nated, and his mean Jurassic pole position (MJP), from rocks subjected to more severe laboratory treatment, is also shown in Fig. 4. The results of this preliminary study show that there are significant differences in remanent magnetisation directions between different in- trusions into the Sydney Basin. They are consist- ent with a hypothesis that the intrusions into the Sydney Basin came in several pulses (Manwaring, 1963) that can be differentiated, in some cases, by differences in their magnetisation directions and the pole positions calculated from them. On the other hand, Hamilton et al (1970) suggest that, on the evidence of coal reflectance figures from fragments found in these breccias, the temper- ature of formation must have been less than 100°C. Two possible solutions to this inconsistency may be considered. Firstly, the temperature within the breccias may have varied from less than 100° to more than 400°C at the time of consolidation. Secondly, chemical alterations in the low temperature ranges may have caused the formation of magnetic minerals, most probably iron oxides that acquired a chemical remanence which itself had higher blocking temperatures. It is not possible to tell how much of secular variation has been averaged by the time spread of the samples, as the rate at which the acquisition of the magnetisation spread through the deposits is not known. Hence an unknown, but probably small, secular variation error is likely to be present in all the results. Bearing this in mind, Figure 3. The results of this preliminary study show that there are significant differences in remanent magnetisation directions between different in- trusions into the Sydney Basin. On the other hand, Hamilton et al (1970) suggest that, on the evidence of coal reflectance figures from fragments found in these breccias, the temper- ature of formation must have been less than 100°C. Two possible solutions to this inconsistency may be considered. Firstly, the temperature within the breccias may have varied from less than 100° to more than 400°C at the time of consolidation. Secondly, chemical alterations in the low temperature ranges may have caused the formation of magnetic minerals, most probably iron oxides that acquired a chemical remanence which itself had higher blocking temperatures. It is not possible to tell how much of secular variation has been averaged by the time spread of the samples, as the rate at which the acquisition of the magnetisation spread through the deposits is not known. Hence an unknown, but probably small, secular variation error is likely to be present in all the results. Bearing this in mind, Figure 3. On the other hand, Hamilton et al (1970) suggest that, on the evidence of coal reflectance figures from fragments found in these breccias, the temper- ature of formation must have been less than 100°C. Two possible solutions to this inconsistency may be considered. Firstly, the temperature within the breccias may have varied from less than 100° to more than 400°C at the time of consolidation. Secondly, chemical alterations in the low temperature ranges may have caused the formation of magnetic minerals, most probably iron oxides that acquired a chemical remanence which itself had higher blocking temperatures. The results are based on a limited number of sites, but the extensive experimental work performed seems to indicate that the Lower Paleozoic picture is much more con~plex than the simple one that could be inferred from the presently liniited data base (Fig. 1). Many specimens carry two distinct remanences; each or both often having dual polarity. Vector diagrams such as those ~rsed by Roy and Park (1974) were found to be most useful for the recognition and analysis of these re- manences. Enlarging the scale near the origin did provide one with much information about the weaker of the two remanences. Diagrams describ- ing the changes of both the horizontal component and, most importantly, the total intensity vectors are shown to be a valuable visual aid for detailed vector analysis. These Cretaceous basic alkalic plutons are distri- buted along an east-west trending belt that is -250 km long by 50 km wide (Fig. I). It coincides with the eastward extension of the Ottawa graben across the St. Lawrence Lowlands and into the Appalachians, and it may be part of a 1500 km zone of intermittent alkalic intrusion over the past 600 Ma (Kumarapeli and Saul1 1966). The fault pattern within the belt appears to control the loca- tion of the plutons (Philpotts 1969). The host rocks include Grenville granitic gneisses in inliers at the west end of the bel

te, and to normal quartz differentiates including gran- ites and bearing Ca plagioclase. Similarly, the plu- tons change form. Passive intrusion becomes in- creasingly important and dominates in the east, giving differentiated zoned plutons surrounded by dikes, ring dikes, cone sheets, and sills. Every specimen was AF demagnetized in steps at 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, and, for about half the specimens, 24 kA/m (Table 1) using a Schonstedt GSD-I de- magnetizer and its remanence remeasured after each step. AF Step Demagnetization Results Virtually all of the specimens behaved in the same manner on AF demagnetization. Figure 2 shows the decay of the site mean intensities for a representative one-third of the sites. Most speci- mens have NRM intensities ranging from -0.1- 20 A/m. They undergo rapid, roughly exponential decay up to - 12 or 16 kA/m as fairly stable, nor- mal, viscous remanent magnetizations (VRM) are removed. Most curves then flatten to indicate a slower exponential decay rate as a more stable, normal, remanent magnetization is uncovered. At 20 or 24 kA/m this stable remanence is generally only 5- 10% of the NRM intensity. The stable rem- anence is believed to be primary and acquired dur- ing cooling of the intrusions as a thermoremanent magnetization (TRM). The remanence may also be, in part, a primary chemical remanent magneti- zation (CRM), partial TRM or partial CRM. The NRM directions generally cluster around the Recent direction of 0°, 65". Upon demagnetization they swing anticlockwise to their primary direc- tion. A few examples are shown in Fig. 3. Reversed remanence directions were found in one or two specimens from each of four sites (17, 18, 32, and 37) and all specimens from one site (36).

Located in its northeastern end, the Notre Dame Bay area (Figs. 1, 2) comprises a sequence of vol- canic and clnstic rocks which are cut by gzzbbro; these are then intruded by numerous lamprophyre dikes of Cretaceous age. The age of the Leading Tickles dunite which intrudes the Ordovician Wild Bight Group has been the subject of a divergence. Both Jurassic and Ordovician ages have been sug- gested. The Exploits Group which includes the Point Leamington Formation, consists of greywacke and argillite (Williams 1962). The Leading Tickles dunite is about 1 km long and about 0.5 km wide, and is well exposed along the road to Leading Tickles settlement. It can be best described as a differentiated diabase stock with an olivine rich zone. This intrusion was named by Helwig (1967) and was interpreted as Jurassic in age based on correlation with the Budgell Harbour Gabbro and related lamprophyres. However, using geochemical and petrographical work as a correla- tive factor, Harris (1973) suggested an Ordovician age for the Leading Tickles dunite. The lamprophyres dikes were first described by Hey1 (1935) as monchiquites and fourchites, al- though Helwig (1967) indicated that the most com- mon are vogesite, spessartite, and kersantite. They range from minor veinlets to dikes 1 m in thickness, most of them being vertical to subvertical, and dominantly northeast trending. The Jurassic-Cretaceous (1 10- 150 Ma) and the Cretaceous-Tertiary (50-81 Ma) boundary are characterized by atnixed polarity interval. It is then probable that the lamprophyre dikes were intruded during the Cretaceous normal (81- 110 Ma) polarity interval. It should be noted that an alternative ex- planation would be that the dikes were intruded in a normal polarity time within a mixed polarity inter- val. This explanation implies that the time of intru- sion and the cooling rate of these dikes were rapid and it would also imply that no chemically acquired remanences are present. Since this explanation is more demanding, the previous explanation is favoured. So, if the dikes were intruded in the nor- mal polarity interval, then the Mont Megantic (172"E, 69"N) and the Monteregian Hills paleopoles (203"E, 65"N and 190°E, 71°N, Larochelle 1968) are probably slightly older than the Notre Dame Bay lamprophyre dikes. Their results show mixed polarities, associating the intrusions with the Juras- sic-Cretaceous mixed polarity interval. Located in its northeastern end, the Notre Dame Bay area (Figs. 1, 2) comprises a sequence of vol- canic and clnstic rocks which are cut by gzzbbro; these are then intruded by numerous lamprophyre dikes of Cretaceous age. The age of the Leading Tickles dunite which intrudes the Ordovician Wild Bight Group has been the subject of a divergence. Both Jurassic and Ordovician ages have been sug- gested. The lamprophyre dikes and the Leading Tickles dunite were sampled for a paleomagnetic study to define the age of magnetization and the tectonic implications of their emplacements. 'Con

The Exploits Group which includes the Point Leamington Formation, consists of greywacke and argillite (Williams 1962). The Leading Tickles dunite is about 1 km long and about 0.5 km wide, and is well exposed along the road to Leading Tickles settlement. It can be best described as a differentiated diabase stock with an olivine rich zone. This intrusion was named by Helwig (1967) and was interpreted as Jurassic in age based on correlation with the Budgell Harbour Gabbro and related lamprophyres. However, using geochemical and petrographical work as a correla- tive factor, Harris (1973) suggested an Ordovician age for the Leading Tickles dunite. They range from minor veinlets to dikes 1 m in thickness, most of them being vertical to subvertical, and dominantly northeast trending. The Jurassic-Cretaceous (1 10- 150 Ma) and the Cretaceous-Tertiary (50-81 Ma) boundary are characterized by atnixed polarity interval. It is then probable that the lamprophyre dikes were intruded during the Cretaceous normal (81- 110 Ma) polarity interval. It should be noted that an alternative ex- planation would be that the dikes were intruded in a normal polarity time within a mixed polarity inter- val. This explanation implies that the time of intru- sion and the cooling rate of these dikes were rapid and it would also imply that no chemically acquired remanences are present. Since this explanation is more demanding, the previous explanation is favoured. So, if the dikes were intruded in the nor- mal polarity interval, then the Mont Megantic (172"E, 69"N) and the Monteregian Hills paleopoles (203"E, 65"N and 190°E, 71°N, Larochelle 1968) are probably slightly older than the Notre Dame Bay lamprophyre dikes. Their results show mixed polarities, associating the intrusions with the Juras- sic-Cretaceous mixed polarity interval. From 16 sites, 197 specimens were subjected to stepwise thermal treatments to 710°C, and a further 46 to incremental af cleaning to 290 mT. The 10 sites from the unshocked St-Urbain anorthosite carry a magnetization with unblocking temperatures (TUB) generally between 600-625°C. with a significant fraction of remanence with TUB > 670°C. Similarly, most of the remanence has a resistive coercive force (rcf) of 100-175 mT, with a significant fraction exceed- ing 290 mT. The remanence is carried by two exsolution phases of titano-hematite, with the later and more hematite-rich lamellae having the higher TUB and rcf. Although only one direction exists, at two sites where intensities are somewhat lower and some natural remanent magnetiza- tion (NRM) directions scattered, treatment reveals a dual polarity remanence. The pole (154"E, 02"s) obtained from these unshocked St-Urbain anorthosite sites falls on a well estab- lished segment of the late Precambrian apparent polar path of suitable age (~950 Ma). Significant results could not be o6tained from three additional sites in the marginal zone due to their ready acquisition of a viscous magnetization following thermal treat

uld not be o6tained from three additional sites in the marginal zone due to their ready acquisition of a viscous magnetization following thermal treatments. Data from two sites which display no shock effects and lie near the margin of the central uplift, and from one highly shocked sample from the crater centre show some possible effects of the shock event. All three have intensities substantially lower than in the St-Urbain sites, which is interpreted in the case of at least one of these sites as a shock-diminished remanence. A puzzling feature of the highly shocked samples is that the phase with a texture reminiscent of the ilmenite-hematite exsolution in the unshocked anorthosites, contains no iron. The remaining remanence, whose direction is parallel with that of the unshocked sites, is interpreted as pre- crater rather than shock-produced. Although many instances have been reported of a new shock-induced remanence imparted to rocks of equivalent and even lesser shock grade than those examined at Charlevoix, in all cases the magnetic carrier seems to have been magnetite. The lack of a shock-induced (emanence at Charlevoix is attributed to the high TUB and rcf of hematite in these rocks. From 16 sites, 197 specimens were subjected to stepwise thermal treatments to 710°C, and a further 46 to incremental af cleaning to 290 mT. The 10 sites from the unshocked St-Urbain anorthosite carry a magnetization with unblocking temperatures (TUB) generally between 600-625°C. with a significant fraction of remanence with TUB > 670°C. Similarly, most of the remanence has a resistive coercive force (rcf) of 100-175 mT, with a significant fraction exceed- ing 290 mT. The remanence is carried by two exsolution phases of titano-hematite, with the later and more hematite-rich lamellae having the higher TUB and rcf. well estab- lished segment of the late Precambrian apparent polar path of suitable age (~950 Ma). Significant results could not be o6tained from three additional sites in the marginal zone due to their ready acquisition of a viscous magnetization following thermal treatments. Data from two sites which display no shock effects and lie near the margin of the central uplift, and from one highly shocked sample from the crater centre show some possible effects of the shock event. All three have intensities substantially lower than in the St-Urbain sites, which is interpreted in the case of at least one of these sites as a shock-diminished remanence. A puzzling feature of the highly shocked samples is that the phase with a texture reminiscent of the ilmenite-hematite exsolution in the unshocked anorthosites, contains no iron. The remaining remanence, whose direction is parallel with that of the unshocked sites, is interpreted as pre- crater rather than shock-produced. In the Shelley Lake granite, an average 35% of the NRM is carried by a mineral with Curie point between 250 and 300°C, 60% by a mineral with blocking temperatures from 300-580°C and a Curie point between 525 and 580°C, and 5% has blocking temperatures >600"C. The regional grade of metamorphism in the southern geotraverse area is middle to upper green- schist. Even this relatively mild degree of meta- morphism has profoundly affected the magnetic minerals. Basalts forming in the oceans today and fresh Tertiary basalts in general have magnetite or titanomagnetite contents of 1% or so, induced magnetizations of - lop3 emu cmP3, and en's > 1 (often >> 1). Their NRM's tend to be about 10 times those of related mafic intrusive rocks. The meta: volcanic rocks in Table 1 have emu I k I emu ~m-~: they contain 10 to 1000 times less magnetite than their modern-day equivalents. On average, their en's are very low, indicating a coarse grain size. Greenschist-facies metamorphism has been responsible for destroying the finer-grained, high-stability fraction of the magnetic minerals in the volcanics. Mafic intrusives have fared some- what better, presumably because of their larger initial grain sizes. Their k and JNRM values are about twice those of the volcanics. It is more difficult to say what magnetic minerals may have been added to these rocks in the course of metamorphism. The felsic intrusives as a class are remarkably magnetic (Table I), although the sampling procedure of course has the bias that the more magnetic formations are sampled in more detail. Group 1 directions tend to have north (or south) declinations and intermediate (40-65") inclinations. Group 2 directions tend to have shal- low inclinations with east to northeast (or west to southwest) declinations. Reversals of the paleofield are recorded in both groups. The proportion of normal and reversed samples is variable and not close to 50:50, suggesting infrequent reversals. A few formations show only group 1 or only group 2 NRM's, but most have examples of both, frequently superimposed in individual samples. Superimposed (or multicomponent) NRM's were separable in two cases: (I) if one component was completely demagnetized at high AF steps, so that the remanence vector reached a stable endpoint direction or (2) if one component was not demag- netized at all over some AF range, usually at low AF steps, so that the direction of the other compo- nent could be deduced by the Zijderveld diagram vector-subtraction technique (Zijderveld 1967). Otherwise, although the magnetization vector fol- lowed a "remagnetization circle" (Halls 1976) joining groups 1 and 2, neither component could be isolated from the data and used in defining the mean group directions. Although there are no radiometric age data for the dikes, Aldrich et al. (1965) report a whole-rock K-Ar age of 960 Ma for an unmetamorphosed diabase dike in Iron County south of Baraga County. If this dike is coeval with the main swarm, then the Baraga-Marquette dikes are Keweenawan in age. The relative age of the dike swarm can be defined within broad limits based on geological field relations. They intrude both the Archean and Animikean rocks and show distinct chilled margins (Graham 1953; Gair and Thaden 1968; Cannon and Klasner 1972). Petrologically the dikes have not been affected by the last post-Animikean meta- morphism at about 1.7Ga ago (Van Schmus and Woolsley 1975). Although there are no radiometric age data for the dikes, Aldrich et al. (1965) report a whole-rock K-Ar age of 960 Ma for an unmetamorphosed diabase dike in Iron County south of Baraga County. If this dike is coeval with the main swarm, then the Baraga-Marquette dikes are Keweenawan in age. The relative age of the dike swarm can be defined within broad limits based on geological field relations. They intrude both the Archean and Animikean rocks and show distinct chilled margins (Graham 1953; Gair and Thaden 1968; Cannon and Klasner 1972). Petrologically the dikes have not been affected by the last post-Animikean meta- morphism at about 1.7Ga ago (Van Schmus and Woolsley 1975). In places the diabase is porphyritic and on freshly broken surfaces the phenocrysts resemble fish scales (Gair and Thaden 1968). Plagioclase and pyroxene are the major minerals with subsidiary biotite, quartz, and olivine. Primary subhedral titanomagnetite is the main opaque mineral, al- though pyrite, ilmenite, and a coloured iron-oxide (presumably hematite) are occasionally present. Secondary alteration is minor but locally strong alteration has occurred (Gair and Thaden 1968; Puffet 1974). Common secondary minerals are chlorite, sericite, and epidote presumably formed as a result of deuteric alteration (Gair and Thaden 1968; L. Schutts, personal communication, 1977). The older dikes (e.g., sites R4, R5, R14 in Fig. 1) are a more greenish diabase with a salmon-coloured groundmass. The dikes in Baraga County are slightly more altered than most of those in Mar- quette County and thus may belong to the older type of diabase. Magnetic Mineralogy Eight thin sections of sites from two sites each of the northwest-up, north-up, and north-northeast- down groups of magnetic directions were examined with a microscope. The rocks are plagiophyric basalts which sometimes contain augite pheno- crysts. Large amygdules and interstitial openings are filled with chlorite, quartz, epidote, and pre- hnite, and suggest shallow water or subaerial extru- sion. Metamorphism corresponds to pumpel- lyite-prehnite or low-greenschist facies. Pyroxene is generally replaced by amphibole. Magnetite is fairly abundant and is variably altered to sphene but in most cases alteration is minor. In detail, the samples showing the north- northeast-down magnetization (e.g., site 69) dis- play relatively strong alteration with all pyroxene replaced by amphibole. In contrast to this, all sam- ples from sites 50 and 51 show only weak alteration of pyroxenes (northwest-up direction) with some oxydization of magnetite to possibly haematite. The samples from site 58 and 59 showing the north-up direction show very similar features to those from the northwest-up sites. The magnetic mineralogy was also studied with a recording thermomagnet

There are, of course, an infinite number of ways to get these poles to coincide by different combinations of northward shift and rota- tion which would result in other source areas for the Karmutsen volcanics but these must all include a large northerly directed component of motion. The age of the northwest-up direction occurring in 20% of the sites has not been established, not even with respect to the folding. Only circumstan- tial evidence (high oxydation state, relatively sim- ple magnetic mineralogy, high coercivity single component) suggests that it might be authentic. However, even if it is secondary, comparison with the post-Triassic part of the apparent polar wander curve for cratonic North America shows an even larger anomaly which then might suggest an even larger northward movement of the area in a shorter time span. These oceanic rocks are separated from Paleozoic and Mesozoic continental rocks to the east by an inferred major fault boundary beneath Cenozoic sedimentary rocks and the Pacific Ocean [Sedlock et al., 1993]. Unmetamorphosed Creta- ceous strata unconformably overlie Late Triassic to Late Juras- sic island arc and ophiolitic rocks that, in turn, structurally overlie coherent blueschists along shallowly dipping normal fault systems [Sedlock, 1988, 1993, 1996]. The Cretaceous strata include terrigenous sandstone, shale, and conglomerate that probably accumulated as turbidites in a forearc basin or basins. In the Cedros-Vizcaino area they are currently assigned to the Albian-Eocene Valle Group [Smith et al., 1993; D. Smith, unpublished data, 1993]. Turbidites in the Magdalena-Santa Margarita area (Figure 1), here informally referred to as the Magdalena Group, strongly resemble the Valle Group, but crop out less extensively and have not been studied in detail. Turbidites in the Magdalena-Santa Margarita area (Figure 1), here informally referred to as the Magdalena Group, strongly resemble the Valle Group, but crop out less extensively and have not been studied in detail. Like the Valle Group, the Mag- dalena Group shows evidence of terrigenous provenance and deposition in deep-sea fan systems. Magdalena Group strata crop out on southern Magdalena Island and in several small, isolated areas on Santa Margarita Island. For this study, palcomagnetic samples were collected from the two thickest exposures at the eastern end of the major east-west arroyo on southern Magdalena Island (MG1) and in the sea cliff of Cerro Colorado on northern Santa Margarita Island (MG2). Shale beds about 90 m above the base of the section contain early Aptian foraminifera (R. Sedlock, unpublished data, 1993), indicating that at least part of the Magdalena Group is older than the Valle Group. Most contacts with adjacent Mesozoic units are faults, but shale locally conformably over- lies and grades downward into tuffaceous siltstone of a mag- matic arc complex of probable Late Jurassic to Early Creta- ceous age. At site MG2, Magdalena Group strata underlying Cerro Colorado form a fault-bounded <100-m-thick section of interbedded sandstone and shale. No age-distinctive microfos- sils were collected from this area, so biostratigraphic correla- tion with the section on Magdalena Island is not possible. However, the base of the section lies concordantly on volcani- clastic and pebbly sandstones of an undated magmatic arc complex. This lithologic similarity to the section 10 km to the west on Magdalena Island may indicate that the Cerro Colorado strata are also, at least in part, Aptian in age. The stratigraphy and structure of the Belcher Islands are well established and they, therefore, represent excellent paleo- magnetic targets since little is known, with cer- tainty, of the origin or paleomagnetism of this geos yncline. The oldest igneous unit, the Eskimo Formation, is comprised of up to about 1000 m of basalts (and some inter- bedded sediments) outcropping as inliers in the cores of the main islands (Fig. 1). The next igneous unit, the Flaherty Formation, is separated from the Eskimo Formation by a thick sedimentary pile and consists of up to 2000 m of basalts and intervening sedimentary-pyroclastic sequences. The Haig in- trusions, which are medium-grained diabases, in- trude all units below, but none above, the Flaherty Fsrmation, and are "probably related to the vol- canic activity represented by the Flaherty Forma- tion" (Dimroth et al. 1970). Another minor intru- sive unit is apparently much younger than the other units of the Belcher Islands and has not been in- cluded in the present study (Hoffmann and Jackson 1969). leomagnetic results from the Karmutsen Formation and sug- gested that, in the Late Triassic, Vancouver Island was situated several thousands of kilometres south of its present position relative to North America (Irving and Yole 1972). Results from 11 sites in the Buttle Lake area (Fig. 1) showed that Karmutsen rocks contain a magnetization (here called X but referred to in our original paper as B) with direc- tions grossly incompatible with the expected geomagnetic field for this region in the Late Trias- sic. The X magnetizations are consistent in direc- tion through a great stratigraphic thickness and are characterized by high unblocking temperatures and fields (coercivities). The unblocking temperatures and fields are a measure of the "hardness" of the remanent magnetization (Zijderveld 1975). We ar- gued that X was the original magnetization ac- quired at the time the rocks were formed. We also showed that other magnetizations (here called Y but referred to previously as A) with less consistent directions and lower unblocking temperatures and fields were present. We argued that Y was a secon- dary overprint, probably acquired during the Juras- sic, because it was less hard and because the direc- tions were roughly along the expected Jurassic field. Samples were collected from the Akaitcho River Formation which represents a small fraction of the Great Slave Supergroup - a sequence of some 8000 m of sedimentary rocks deposited be- tween about 2200 and 1800 Ma ago. Earth Sci., 17, 1583-1588 (1980) [Traduit par le journal] Introduction The occurrence of minor igneous intrusions in the Valley and Ridge province of Virginia and West Virginia has long been known (Darton and Diller 1890; Darton and Keith 1898). The intrusions are mostly northwest-striking dikes, cutting tightly folded limestone, shales, and sandstones of Or- dovician to Devonian age (Fig. 1). Although the intrusions of Pendleton County, West Virginia are predominately basalts, a wide variety of igneous rock types are represented; in Highland County, Virginia, andesites are more numerous. On the basis of petrographic resemblances to other eastern North American dikes, Garner (1956) assumed the basalts to be of Triassic age. The andesites had been postulated to be related to the Devonian Tioga bentonite. It came as a surprise, therefore, when Fullagar and Bottino (1969) determined an Eocene age for biotites from the andesite. Several geophysical anomalies are located near the Eocene rocks and may be causally related to them (Dennison and Johnson 1971; Bollinger and Gilbert 1974). These include the most extensive concentration of thermal springs in eastern North America, an 'earthquake shadow zone' with re- duced surface disturbances associa

on and Johnson 1971) have noted that the intrusions are situated along a long lasting, deep seated zone of crustal weakness. The recognition of olivine basalts as contem- poraneous with the more felsic rocks makes Denni- son and Johnson's (1971) argument for derivation from a granitic pluton appear dubious, while Hall's (1974) proposal for fractional crystallization of a basaltic magma is strengthened. The Eocene magnetic directions obtained from units of volcanic breccia and diatreme suggest a shallow depth of dike emplacement and possible volcanism. 1588 CAN. J. EARTH SCI. Subsequent K-Ar dating, however, has shown this dike to be about 46Ma old and this direction has therefore been included in our mean result. The dike is slightly altered to the extent that olivine has been replaced by antigorite (Garner 1956), and secondary magne- tite may have formed during the serpentinization process. Alternately, the dike may have acquired its magnetization during an excursion. This latter possibility seems especially attractive in light of the rapid polarity reversal rate during the Eocene (Heirtzler et al. 1968). However, one of the more notable results of this study is that no nor- mally magnetized units were found, although Lgv- lie and Opdyke (1974) found two normal andesites. Except for one possible anomalous age (site 8, 34.2 Ma), the K-Ar ages of the intrusions are in the range 42 to 46 Ma. MCMURRY, AND M. E. EVANS Institute of Earth and Planetary Physics, University of Alberta, Edmonton, Alta., Canada T6G 2JI Received July 7, 1980 Revision accepted November 6, 1980 Results are reported from 59 stratigraphic horizons spanning an aggregate of some 2000 m of sedimentary rocks of the Great Slave Supergroup, mostly located in the Kahochella Group. Partial demagnetization experiments and vector differences indicate that the magnetization involved is multicomponent, with a well-defined overprint masking an underlying magnetic component. The overprint has now been recognized in many formations of the Great Slave Supergroup and is interpreted as having been acquired in response to uplift and cooling following orogeny in the Coronation Geosyncline. It corresponds to a paleomagnetic pole at 9I0W, 2I0N (A95 = 5'). Removal of this overprint reveals the underlying, presumed primary, magnetization, which has a mean direction of D = 129", I = + 2 lo (N = 18 sites, k = 12, a95 = 10") and a corresponding pole at 62OW, 7"s (K = 15, Ag5 = 9"). A third population of components, K3, has low blocking temperature and coercivity and is isolated only by chemical leaching. K3 has steep positive inclination, northern declination, and is post-tectonic. It is interpreted as a recent magnetization. Any interpretation of the path of apparent polar wander for North America must accommodate the sequence of magnetization K1 to K2. The timing of tectonism in the Keweenawan basin is bracketed by the times of acquisition of K1 and K2. These results reconfirm some recent interpretations that include Grenville poles on the polar wander trackof interior Laurentia. The stratigraphy and petrology of the Fond du Lac Formation have been summarized by Morey (1967) and much of the following description is from that work. The Fond du Lac Formation consists of subarkosic and arko- sic shales, siltstones, and sandstones with a basal con- glomerate, probably representing a wedge of clastic material deposited in an oxidizing deltaic environment. These rocks crop out in a limited area along the St. Louis River and a small tributary, Mission Creek, near Duluth, Minnesota (Fig. 1). The Fond du Lac exceeds 244 m in thickness, but only 90 m is now exposed. The red color is due to hematite, which occurs as a coating on the surfaces of sand- and silt-sized quartz and feldspar grains or occupying the interstices between the grains. Hematite was probably formed in place, sometime after deposition and prior to complete lithification. A further source of hematite may be the alteration of detrital iron-bearing silicate minerals such as pyroxene, horn- blende, and biotite. Linearity of a demagnetization trajectory on an orthogonal projection may be regarded as a determination of the spectral window of demagne- tization over which a component is isolated (Dunlop 1979). Components, so determined, were isolated by vector subtraction of the two results that best defined the linear trajectory. For example, refemng to Fig. 2b, one component is isolated by vector subtraction of the re- manences measured after treatments of 550 and 640°C, and a second component is isolated by subtraction of the remanences measured after treatments of 650 and 670°C. Components were classified on the basis of coercivity, blocking temperature, and resistance to leaching. With the exception of a single site in the Fond du Lac Formation, there was good correlation between the directions and the physical properties of the compo- nents. Components with high blocking temperatures (650-670°C) and coercivities greater than 100 mT and that resist leaching in 8 N HC1 for up to 50-100 h were found in nearly all samples. Components with these properties were assigned to the K1 population. A second set of components, assigned to the K2 population, had blocking temperatures between 400 and 640°C, coerci- vities greater than 100 mT, and were the first compo- nents to be removed by leaching. K2 was present in the Fond du Lac and Middle River samples, but absent from the Eileen. In almost every case, K2 was found coexist- ing with K1 in the same specimen. A third set of compo- nents,

As was the case for the Fond du Lac, the Middle River K2 population isolated by leaching has systematically lower inclinations compared with the K2 isolated thermally. Again, this is attributed to simul- taneous removal of K1 and K2. Comparing Fig. 6c with Fig. 3 c, the Fond du Lac K2 is predominantly of polarity opposite to the Middle River K2 before structural correc- tion. An argument will be presented favouring a post- tectonic age for the Middle River K2. The Middle River K3 population is plotted without structural correction in Fig. 4b. This population clusters about the present field direction; structural correction carries the mean to a direction similar to certain North American Ordovician magnetizations. However, this is not consistent with a pre-Late Cambrian age of de- formation in the Keweenawan Basin. It is concluded that the Middle River K3 is post-tectonic. Thin-section examination shows an abundance of de- trital opaque grains remaining after chemical leaching, as was the case for the Fond du Lac Formation. Since a post-tectonic age of magnetization is not consistent with a detrital magnetization and because of the comparative- ly low blocking temperatures and coercivities of the Fond du Lac and Middle River K3 populations, K3 is interpreted to be a very recent viscous magnetization acquired in the present field. Linearity of a demagnetization trajectory on an orthogonal projection may be regarded as a determination of the spectral window of demagne- tization over which a component is isolated (Dunlop 1979). Components, so determined, were isolated by vector subtraction of the two results that best defined the linear trajectory. For example, refemng to Fig. 2b, one component is isolated by vector subtraction of the re- manences measured after treatments of 550 and 640°C, and a second component is isolated by subtraction of the remanences measured after treatments of 650 and 670°C. Components were classified on the basis of coercivity, blocking temperature, and resistance to leaching. With the exception of a single site in the Fond du Lac Formation, there was good correlation between the directions and the physical properties of the compo- nents. Components with high blocking temperatures (650-670°C) and coercivities greater than 100 mT and that resist leaching in 8 N HC1 for up to 50-100 h were found in nearly all samples. Components with these properties were assigned to the K1 population. A second set of components, assigned to the K2 population, had blocking temperatures between 400 and 640°C, coerci- vities greater than 100 mT, and were the first compo- nents to be removed by leaching. The sequence of magnetiza- tion is consistent with those interpretations that include the Grenville poles on the polar wander track of Interior Laurentia. Comparing poles calculated from pre- and post-tectonic magnetizations in the Keweenawan to dated poles from igneous and metamorphic rock units yields an estimate of the time of deformation in the Keweenawan Basin. Geology of the Upper Keweenawan Cropping out along the south shore of Lake Superior and various natural exposures along streams and rivers in northern Wisconsin, Michigan, and east-central Min- nesota is a thick (5000m) accumulation of terrestrial conglomerates, sandstones, siltstones, and shales gener- ally assigned to the Upper Keweenawan. The strati- graphic position of these rocks is poorly determined because of the complete absence of a fossil record and limited exposure due to the cover of Pleistocene drift. It is known that these rocks overlie the ca. llOOMa Keweenawan basalts and, in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan, are overlain by Upper Cambrian sediments. The stratigraphy and petrology of the Fond du Lac Formation have been summarized by Morey (1967) and much of the following description is from that work. The Fond du Lac Formation consists of subarkosic and arko- sic shales, siltstones, and sandstones with a basal con- glomerate, probably representing a wedge of clastic material deposited in an oxidizing deltaic environment. These rocks crop out in a limited area along the St. Louis River and a small tributary, Mission Creek, near Duluth, Minnesota (Fig. 1). The Fond du Lac exceeds 244 m in thickness, but only 90 m is now exposed. The red color is due to hematite, which occurs as a coating on the surfaces of sand- and silt-sized quartz and feldspar grains or occupying the interstices between the grains. Hematite was probably formed in place, sometime after deposition and prior to complete lithification. A further source of hematite may be the alteration of detrital iron-bearing silicate minerals such as pyroxene, horn- blende, and biotite. The correlation and absolute age of the Fond du Lac Formation have long been problems. Linearity of a demagnetization trajectory on an orthogonal projection may be regarded as a determination of the spectral window of demagne- tization over which a component is isolated (Dunlop 1979). Components, so determined, were isolated by vector subtraction of the two results that best defined the linear trajectory. For example, refemng to Fig. 2b, one component is isolated by vector subtraction of the re- manences measured after treatments of 550 and 640°C, and a second component is isolated by subtraction of the remanences measured after treatments of 650 and 670°C. Components were classified on the basis of coercivity, blocking temperature, and resistance to leaching. With the exception of a single site in the Fond du Lac Formation, there was good correlation between the directions and the physical properties of the compo- nents. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: a- ture of the Upper Keweenawan rocks investigated in this study is very similar to that reported from certain rocks in the Grenville Province. The sequence of magnetiza- tion is consistent with those interpretations that include the Grenville poles on the polar wander track of Interior Laurentia. Comparing poles calculated from pre- and post-tectonic magnetizations in the Keweenawan to dated poles from igneous and metamorphic rock units yields an estimate of the time of deformation in the Keweenawan Basin. Geology of the Upper Keweenawan Cropping out along the south shore of Lake Superior and various natural exposures along streams and rivers in northern Wisconsin, Michigan, and east-central Min- nesota is a thick (5000m) accumulation of terrestrial conglomerates, sandstones, siltstones, and shales gener- ally assigned to the Upper Keweenawan. The Fond du Lac Formation consists of subarkosic and arko- sic shales, siltstones, and sandstones with a basal con- glomerate, probably representing a wedge of clastic material deposited in an oxidizing deltaic environment. These rocks crop out in a limited area along the St. Louis River and a small tributary, Mission Creek, near Duluth, Minnesota (Fig. 1). The Fond du Lac exceeds 244 m in thickness, but only 90 m is now exposed. The red color is due to hematite, which occurs as a coating on the surfaces of sand- and silt-sized quartz and feldspar grains or occupying the interstices between the grains. Linearity of a demagnetization trajectory on an orthogonal projection may be regarded as a determination of the spectral window of demagne- tization over which a component is isolated (Dunlop 1979). Components, so determined, were isolated by vector subtraction of the two results that best defined the linear trajectory. Components were classified on the basis of coercivity, blocking temperature, and resistance to leaching. With the exception of a single site in the Fond du Lac Formation, there was good correlation between the directions and the physical properties of the compo- nents. K2 is found in the Fond du Lac Formation and the Middle River section, but is absent from the Eileen. It is post-tectonic, acquired after the tilting of the Middle River section. The K3 population was resolved only by leaching. It is characterized by blocking temperatures between 300 and 400°C and coercivities from 10 to 50 mT. The Fond du Lac Formation consists of subarkosic and arko- sic shales, siltstones, and sandstones with a basal con- glomerate, probably representing a wedge of clastic material deposited in an oxidizing deltaic environment. These rocks crop out in a limited area along the St. Louis River and a small tributary, Mission Creek, near Duluth, Minnesota (Fig. 1). Linearity of a demagnetization trajectory on an orthogonal projection may be regarded as a determination of the spectral window of demagne- tization over which a component is isolated (Dunlop 1979). Components, so determined, were isolated by vector subtraction of the two results that best defined the linear trajectory. For example, refemng to Fig. 2b, one component is isolated by vector subtraction of the re- manences measured after treatments of 550 and 640°C, and a second component is isolated by subtraction of the remanences measured after treatments of 650 and 670°C. Components were classified on the basis of coercivity, blocking temperature, and resistance to leaching. With the exception of a single site in the Fond du Lac Formation, there was good correlation between the directions and the physical properties of the compo- nents. Components with high blocking temperatures (650-670°C) and coercivities greater than 100 mT and that resist leaching in 8 N HC1 for up to 50-100 h were found in nearly all samples. Components with these properties were assigned to the K1 population. A second set of components, assigned to the K2 population, had blocking temperatures between 400 and 640°C, coerci- vities greater than 100 mT, and were the first compo- nents to be removed by leaching. K2 was present in the Fond du Lac and Middle River samples, but absent from the Eileen. In almost every case, K2 was found coexist- ing with K1 in the same specimen. A third set of compo- nents,

The volcanics yield multicomponent magnetizations: a hard characteristic magnetization and a relatively soft one. These components could be separated easily and the intensity decay curves of the different components could also be obtained separately using Zijderveld's method. Three different groups of site-mean characteristic magnetizations can be distinguished, each representing a different stratigraphic level. The paleopoles derived from these magnetizations are, from oldest to youngest, 186"E, 10"s; 173"E, 0I0N; and 154"E, 06"N. This is interpreted as a rapid motion of the paleopole for the North American craton during the Early Cambrian. The paleopole derived from the hard characteristic dyke direction is 123"E, 03"s. This magnetization direction was also found at one of the sites in the volcanics. This means that the contact test is positive and that the hard characteristic magnetization of the dyke is acquired at the time of intrusion. The character- istic magnetization of the Buckingham volcanics is believed to have been acquired during initial cooling of the rock owing to a combination of the following observations: (1) its unblocking temperatures are limited to a narrow window immediately below the Curie point of magnetite (Fig. 6); (2) no other stable component of magnetization is present at temperatures higher than 580°C; (3) its resistance to alternating fields is high (Fig. 7). The volcanics yield multicomponent magnetizations: a hard characteristic magnetization and a relatively soft one. These components could be separated easily and the intensity decay curves of the different components could also be obtained separately using Zijderveld's method. The "aberrancy" of southerly located Siluro-Devonian poles with respect to those in northern latitudes is discussed in the context of possible transcurrent motion of the "Acadia" displaced terrain with respect to cratonic North America. Presently available paleomagnetic data are not conclusive and cannot confirm or negate this possibility. The CB-1, CB-2, and CB-3 poles are interpreted as representing rapid apparent polar wander with respect to Cape Breton Island during Siluro-Devonian time. In the older Cambrian granites, pole CB (37"N, 176"E; Sp, Sm = 2", 3'), derived from a high coercivity (20-70 mT) mean remanence direction NW (D = 318", 1 = +ISo; K = 298, N = 10 sites), probably corresponds to the Avalonian Orogeny. Further results are needed to interpret the paleogeographic setting of the Avalon microcontinent in early Paleozoic time. ng field (AF) and thermal experiments performed on the younger granites indicate that they are characterized by three different mean directions of magnetization in the 10-60 mT coercivity spectra: SE (D = 149", 1 = $70"; K = 160, N = 4 sites); NE-1 (D = 72", 1 = -70"; K = 320, N = 3 sites); andNE-2 (D = 31°, 1 = -24"; K = 67, N = 3 sites) with corresponding paleopole positions at CB-1 (16'N, 41%'; Sp, Sm = 6", 7"); CB-2 (32"N, 97"W; Sp, Sm = 7", 8"); and CB-3 (27"S, 96%'; Sp, Sm = 6", 1 lo). The radiometric ages of these three remanence directions do not differ from each other by more than 50 Ma; these remanences are also present as low coercivity (5-25 mT) magnetizations in the Avalonian granites (10 sites). Antipole CB-3 agrees with other recently reported Early Devonian paleomagnetic results from the northern Appalachians. In contrast, the two other antipoles (CB-1 and CB-2) are located in southerly latitudes but do not differ significantly from poles of contemporaneous rocks in New Brunswick and Newfoundland. The "aberrancy" of southerly located Siluro-Devonian poles with respect to those in northern latitudes is discussed in the context of possible transcurrent motion of the "Acadia" displaced terrain with respect to cratonic North America. The "aberrancy" of southerly located Siluro-Devonian poles with respect to those in northern latitudes is discussed in the context of possible transcurrent motion of the "Acadia" displaced terrain with respect to cratonic North America. Presently available paleomagnetic data are not conclusive and cannot confirm or negate this possibility. The CB-1, CB-2, and CB-3 poles are interpreted as representing rapid apparent polar wander with respect to Cape Breton Island during Siluro-Devonian time. In the older Cambrian granites, pole CB (37"N, 176"E; Sp, Sm = 2", 3'), derived from a high coercivity (20-70 mT) mean remanence direction NW (D = 318", 1 = +ISo; K = 298, N = 10 sites), probably corresponds to the Avalonian Orogeny. Further results are needed to interpret the paleogeographic setting of the Avalon microcontinent in early Paleozoic time. Brunswick and Newfoundland. The "aberrancy" of southerly located Siluro-Devonian poles with respect to those in northern latitudes is discussed in the context of possible transcurrent motion of the "Acadia" displaced terrain with respect to cratonic North America. Presently available paleomagnetic data are not conclusive and cannot confirm or negate this possibility.
